analysis.one_liner: Bans political action committees from federal elections and cuts the individual contribution limit to $100.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Administration Committee and died when the 102nd Congress ended, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have eliminated political action committees — the corporate, union, and trade-association funds that bundle large contributions to federal candidates — by barring any group committee from contributing, soliciting, or spending in federal elections [S3]. It also would have cut the limit on individual contributions to a candidate from $1,000 to $100, forcing candidates to rely on many small donors instead of a few large ones [S2][S3]. The idea was to shrink the role of organized money in congressional elections and make candidates answerable to individual voters rather than interest-group treasuries [S2]. It was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, in the form of candidates who would have to raise money in small amounts from individual constituents rather than in large checks from PACs backed by corporations, unions, and trade associations. Candidates without access to established PAC networks — challengers and outsiders — would also compete on more even footing.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit any political committee other than individuals from contributing, soliciting, or spending money to influence federal elections, ending PAC financing of congressional campaigns [S3].
It would cut the ceiling on individual contributions to a candidate from $1,000 to $100, reducing the weight of any single donor's check [S2][S3].
Together these changes would force candidates for federal office to build support among many small individual contributors rather than organized interest-group committees [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees — corporate, labor, and trade-association — would lose their entire channel for influencing federal elections, and the incumbents and parties that raise most of their money through PACs would lose that funding stream. Candidates would have to raise far more money in far smaller increments.

drawbacks.text: Banning PACs while capping individual gifts at $100 would leave candidates with only very small donations, which can push campaign money into less-tracked channels like independent expenditures and party soft money, where voters can see even less of it.

A $100 limit raises the cost of campaigning dramatically for any candidate, and self-funded wealthy candidates — who can spend their own money without limit — would be relatively advantaged over candidates who must raise dollar by dollar.
Labor unions argue that PACs let working people pool small contributions to match corporate spending power; removing both sides' committees does not automatically make the field more equal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — severing candidates' dependence on interest-group committee money — directly addresses the biggest driver of congressional fundraising, and the $100 individual limit would make any single donation nearly weightless. But the design is blunt: cutting the individual limit to $100 while eliminating PACs leaves a vacuum that money would likely fill through independent expenditures and party committees outside the contribution limits, and it advantages wealthy self-funders. A stronger version would pair the PAC ban with limits on those workarounds.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Romano Mazzoli introduced the bill on April 9, 1992, in the second session of the 102nd Congress [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the same day; that was the last action ever taken on the bill [S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].
The committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the House floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PACs and the incumbents and party committees that depend on PAC money were better off, because the existing campaign finance structure was left completely untouched. Nothing changed: PACs kept their full role in federal elections.

for.name: Rep. Romano L. Mazzoli
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban PAC activities in federal elections and cut the individual contribution limit to $100; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over election law
against.what_they_did: Received the referred bill on April 9, 1992 and took no further action; no hearing, no markup, no report before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and only one sponsor, so no partisan split is visible in the record; the bill never progressed far enough for members to take a position.

industries.industry: Political action committees (corporate, labor, and trade-association)
industries.note: The bill would abolish their role in federal elections entirely, ending the committee-based channel through which organized interests fund congressional campaigns. Their loss would have been the public's gain under the bill's theory, so their interest ran against the reform.

industries.industry: Incumbent lawmakers and party fundraising operations
industries.note: By dying without action, the bill left intact the PAC-driven fundraising system that supplies most incumbent campaign money. The status quo — which the bill was written to dismantle — was preserved.

The existing large-check fundraising system was left unchanged, preserving the business of soliciting and processing big committee contributions. The bill's small-dollar model would have reshaped this industry had it advanced.
